title: Home Blood Pressure Monitors: How to Pick an Easy Upper-Arm Cuff, and What It Can't Tell You
subtitle: A plain-English guide to choosing an upper-arm blood pressure cuff for home, from cuff size and batteries to apps and subscription fees.
excerpt: An automatic upper-arm cuff with one big button is a straightforward choice for tracking blood pressure at home. Here is what to look for, two options from smaller online stores, and what these monitors cannot do.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: A home blood pressure monitor lets you take a reading in your own chair, at your own pace. Your doctor can tell you whether home readings make sense for you and how often to take them.

The tricky part is the crowded shelf: wrist cuffs, finger clips, phone-connected models and some with monthly fees. An automatic upper-arm cuff with a big button and a clear screen is the type the American Heart Association recommends, so it is a sensible place to start.

An automatic monitor has two parts: a soft cuff that wraps around your upper arm and a small box with a screen. You press a button, the cuff squeezes, then slowly loosens while the monitor senses your pulse. It then shows three numbers: systolic (the top number, the pressure when your heart beats), diastolic (the bottom number, the pressure between beats) and your pulse.
AARP reports that the American Heart Association recommends this type of device for home use:
"an automatic, cuff-style, upper arm (biceps) monitor" — American Heart Association, as quoted by AARP

The heart association calls wrist and finger models less reliable. They are a fallback for someone whose arm cannot fit a cuff or finds one too painful, and they are not a good choice as a gift. According to a search summary of AARP's guide, its lab and home testing found the Omron 3 Series and an A&D Medical multi-user monitor to be the most accurate. We could not read the full AARP page, so treat that as a pointer rather than the last word. That finding is for the Omron 3 Series, and we have not tested either monitor below ourselves.
What a home monitor can't tell you

A home monitor gives you a number, not a diagnosis. Some models show a symbol when they detect an irregular heartbeat, but that is a flag to mention to your doctor, not an answer. Omron advises consulting your physician if that symbol appears. A home cuff does not replace medically supervised monitoring, and it will not call for help. As general safety advice, if you ever feel seriously unwell, call 911, and ask your doctor what readings or symptoms should prompt a call to the office.

items: Check cuff size first. The Omron cuff fits upper arms 9 to 17 inches, and Omron also lists an optional smaller cuff for 7 to 17 inches. The Greater Goods page's description gives 8.7 to 16.5 inches. A larger or smaller arm needs a different cuff, sold separately. Ask your doctor, nurse or pharmacist how to measure your arm.
Choose one big start button and a large, easy-to-read screen. A backlit display helps in a dim room.

Check for fees. AARP notes that some premium models, such as the CONNEQT Pulse, need a subscription to share data with your doctor or get deeper insights. Neither product page we read lists a fee, but confirm before you buy.
Count the batteries. Some kits include batteries and a wall adapter. Others do not, so buy them before the first reading.
Think about memory. A monitor that holds a small number of readings works fine alongside a paper notebook. An app can keep a longer history, but it needs a smartphone.
Treat apps as optional. Bluetooth (a short-range wireless link to a phone) can be handy, but pairing may frustrate some people. Both monitors below can take readings without it.

Compare prices and returns. The prices below come from smaller online stores and may differ elsewhere, so check the maker's own site and a large retailer, and confirm the return policy before you buy.

sections.content: Setting It Up and Using It Well

Before the first reading, put in batteries and read the manual or quick-start guide that comes in the box. If you are unsure how to position yourself or the cuff, ask your doctor, nurse or pharmacist to show you.

The Omron shows a movement symbol if you moved during a reading, and an irregular-heartbeat symbol when it detects an irregular rhythm 2 or more times in a reading. Ask your doctor what to do if either appears. Your doctor can also tell you how to use a log of your numbers.

The Omron BP7100 needs 4 AA batteries, which are not in the box. It also stores only 14 readings and deletes the oldest when full, so keep a simple paper log. The Greater Goods kit includes batteries and an AC adapter and can sync readings to a free phone app. That page lists memory as both 120 and 60 readings, so confirm the figure before you buy. We have not independently verified either monitor's accuracy.
sections.label: Before You Buy

sections.content: A good home blood pressure monitor does not need to be fancy. Check your cuff size, choose an upper-arm model with a big button and a clear screen, and look closely at any fees. Then share your numbers with your doctor, who can explain what they mean for you.

products.name: Omron 3 Series BP7100 Upper Arm Blood Pressure Monitor
products.blurb: A one-button monitor with no phone connection, for someone who wants to keep things simple. The cuff fits 9 to 17 inches, it stores 14 readings and it needs 4 AA batteries, which are not included. It flags an irregular heartbeat when detected 2 or more times in a reading. A version of AARP's list names the Omron 3 Series Best Value but notes a short cord and limited storage.

products.name: Greater Goods Bluetooth Smart Upper Arm Blood Pressure Monitor
products.blurb: Suits someone who likes the option of tracking readings in the free Balance Health app, though it can take readings without a phone. It has a large start/stop button and backlit display, and comes with batteries, an AC adapter and a travel case. The page's memory figures conflict, so confirm before buying.
